budget.title: What the saving amount means
budget.intro: The plan needs one explicit basis for the money you add to investments. Pick the one you actually track; the two are not interchangeable.
budget.modeSavingsDetail: You enter the amount left for investing; the two questions below settle exactly what it already takes off.
budget.modeIncomeDetail: You enter working-period spending and the plan draws on your income. Not modelled yet in this slice.
budget.debtIncluded: Does that amount already subtract the loan payments you listed?
budget.debtIncludedDetail: Yes records that the figure already subtracts them, so the plan must not subtract them again.
budget.taxBenefitIncluded: Does it already reflect the RRSP/RRIF tax difference?
budget.taxBenefitIncludedDetail: Yes records that the figure already reflects it, so no refund is added on top.
budget.workingSpendingHint: Enter what you spend in a normal working year, excluding the loan payments listed later. It is not the retirement figure.
budget.legacyReview: This figure came from your earlier plan, where a different definition applied. Choose what it means before it is used.
budget.legacyKeepDetail: Treat the figure as already net of the listed loan payments and without the tax difference. The plan records that, and pricing stays unavailable until the rule exists.
budget.legacyAdopt: Treat it as the new net saving amount
budget.legacyAdoptDetail: Use the same number under the definition above: already net of living costs, tax and the listed loan payments, with no separate tax refund.
budget.legacyBaseline: Your earlier plan also amortised {{annualDebt}} of listed loan payments per year. That baseline is only for comparison; nothing is added to your figure automatically.
budget.stateReady: Ready: net saving amount of {{value}} per year, net of the listed loan payments and of the tax difference.
budget.stateUnknown: Still to answer: {{fields}}. The plan keeps these unknown rather than assuming an answer.
budget.estimateExcluded: The saving basis you recorded leaves out a component this projection still treats as included, so the result below is an estimate rather than a precise number until BE-14 B prices the recorded basis.
budget.fieldDebt: whether the listed loan payments are already subtracted
budget.fieldTax: whether the RRSP/RRIF tax difference is already reflected

be11.ledgerLimit: Annual tax uses the pinned 2026 real-dollar assumptions. Estate tax, other solvers and complex funding events require further person-owned rules.
be11.explanation: The same tax facts apply in Guided and Professional. Enter each person's own balance (registered accounts stay individually owned); the amounts must add up to the household total. Nothing is divided automatically. Working-year tax and unsupported asset events remain estimates.
be11.splitSum: Your amount + partner's amount: {{sum}} of {{total}} CAD
be11.splitMismatch: These two amounts must add up to the account's {{total}} CAD balance. Ownership stays unconfirmed until they match.
be11.splitHelp: Registered accounts are owned by one person each: enter each person's balance, and the two amounts must add up to the household total. Non-registered accounts and properties record each person's share; nothing is divided automatically.
be11.lockedOwnerResetHelp: Changing the locked-in account's owner in the main form re-records the split as 100% to that owner.
be11.spouseSupport: Do you support and live with your spouse for the spouse amount?
be11.splitTransferor: Elective eligible pension split: who transfers?
be11.splitAmount: Annual amount transferred (CAD; at most 50% of eligible income)
be11.rrifFactorCategory: Verified RRIF factor category (check transfer history)
be11.rrifFactorHelp: Check the provider’s opening, transfer and amendment records before choosing a category. Opening year alone does not prove qualification; leave it unconfirmed to keep the exact minimum and tax result limited.

be35.qcSplitTransferor: Quebec Schedule Q election: who transfers?
be35.splitHelp: The Quebec election is separate from the federal pension split. The transferor must be at least 65; choose no transfer unless the Schedule Q election is intended.
be35.coverageHelp: This affects only the Québec prescription-drug premium (TP-1 line 447) in each person’s Québec tax row — nothing else. It applies to Québec residents covered by the public RAMQ plan, an eligible private plan, or a verified exemption. Choose one status for the whole year; the month detail is only needed if coverage actually changed mid-year. A year containing a public month stays a labelled estimate until the 2026 Schedule K is published.
be35.publicLimit: Public premiums use family income and the tax-year Schedule K, which is not yet published for 2026. The July–June RAMQ tariffs are not a full-year tax amount.
be35.limit: Quebec family credits and FSS use 2026 parameters. Public RAMQ months remain unverified until the 2026 Schedule K; other complex tax events remain estimates.
be35.monthDetailHelp: Only needed when coverage changed mid-year. The tax-year premium (Schedule K) reconciles the January–June and July–December periods separately, so the month of a change can matter — the RAMQ maximum rose on 1 July 2026. A public month keeps the Québec tax a labelled estimate until the 2026 Schedule K is published.

tagline: Retire early, the Canadian way - TFSA, RRSP, CPP/QPP and OAS, modelled properly.
ruleAssumptionsPolicy: Published figures take priority. Unpublished future years require an explicit assumption: index eligible nominal thresholds once per year at {{rate}} planning inflation; frozen thresholds stay fixed.
ruleAssumptionsLimit: The federal and provincial rate ladders and basic personal amounts come from the selected rule pack. The per-jurisdiction coverage list above states what those numbers include and exclude. Each cited authority is shown with either the figures a person content-checked against it and the date, or the plain statement that it is listed only and its content was not checked; where a row records a limit — an approximation, a derived rather than published figure, or a page that blocks automated readers — that limit is stated next to the link. The GIS/Allowance fitted reduction and the CCB approximations are unchanged, and no result is a complete tax return or after-benefit position.
ruleCoverageUnsupported: Credits these {{jurisdiction}} numbers do not include:
ruleCoverageNotModelled: Not modelled means not approximated: nothing in the engine stands in for the entries above, so a result is never a complete tax return.
ruleCoverageCaveat: This calculator models the federal and provincial income tax brackets, the basic personal amount and the named credits in this list only. It does not model the GST/HST credit, any provincial or territorial cash benefit, any low-income or refundable tax reduction, dividend tax credits, the Canada employment amount or the net-income base the province-specific spouse-credit worksheets use (the spouse rows price the published maxima and thresholds, not that base), so no figure it produces is a complete tax return, a complete after-tax position, or a complete after-benefit position. Where a credit it does apply is a pinned rather than year-switched figure (the age and pension amounts, the spouse maxima, the Ontario surtax and health premium, probate fees, the capital-gains inclusion rate, the Quebec levies), an assumed future year carries that 2026 figure forward unchanged, and the row says so.
ruleMbConflict: Resolved 2026-09-15. Manitoba's dedicated 2026 CRA guide (T4032-MB, January 2026) governs: its chart lists $47,000/$100,000 at 10.8%/12.75%/17.4% and a $15,780 basic personal amount, all matching this pack. CRA's general rate page lists $47,564/$101,200, which the dedicated guide and Manitoba's 2026 budget (bracket indexation paused for 2026) both contradict. No number changed.
rulePeConflict: Resolved 2026-09-15. Prince Edward Island's dedicated CRA guide (T4032-PE, July 2026) governs: its fourth threshold is $142,520, replacing January's $142,250, and it states that PE's new over-$200,000 bracket is 20% for 2026 and subsequent years (the 21% it also prints is a six-month prorated withholding rate). This pack moves the fourth threshold to $142,520 and keeps 17.62%, 19% and the 20% top rate, so PE provincial tax falls by $3.726 at $142,520 and above, phasing in from nil at $142,250 — the $270 band January charged at 19%.
retirementSpending: Desired after-tax annual spending in retirement
estCppTitle: Not sure? Estimate from work history
estOasTitle: Not sure? Estimate from residence years
estRatio: Average earnings while working, as % of the YMPE cap (2026: ~$74,600)
cppEstUsesFireAge: Uses the FIRE age you entered above ({{age}}) — contributions stop that year.
estResidence: Years lived in Canada by 65 (from age 18)
cppEstNote: Approximates the CPP rule: your best 39 years between 18 and 65 count (the dropout removes 17% of the contributory period). Stopping contributions at FIRE dilutes the average - why early retirees rarely get the maximum. After applying, the calculator also remembers your work history: claiming early (say at 60) shortens the divisor to ~35 years, so zero-income years dilute less - handled automatically. The CPP enhancement (post-2019 contributions) is not modelled, so the estimate leans conservative. Check My Service Canada Account for exact figures.
oasEstNote: OAS is residence-based, not work-based: 40 years in Canada after age 18 gives the full amount, fewer years are prorated (common for immigrants).
coupleNote: Accounts and spending are household totals; tax assumes ideal income splitting between spouses.
accountsHint: Enter today's balances, not the balances you expect at FIRE — the projection grows them from your current age.
pensionAnnual: Annual pension at start age ($/yr, today's dollars, before tax)
pensionNote: Enter the lifetime annual amount from your pension statement (already reduced for an early start, if that applies). DC/LIRA money belongs in the separate Locked DC/LIRA account, not RRSP/RRIF. Payments are taxed as eligible pension income: splittable with a spouse and earning the pension income credit at any age. Not modelled: survivor percentages and Quebec's 65+ provincial splitting restriction.
valPensionWindow: Pension start age should be between {{min}} and {{max}}
valBridgeAfter65: The bridge benefit ends at 65 — starting at 65 or later means it never pays out
lockedRetirementToggle: Use a locked DC pension / LIRA account
lockedRetirementEmployee: Your annual contribution (carved out of annual savings)
lockedRetirementEmployer: Employer annual contribution / match (extra to annual savings)
lockedRetirementAge: Earliest withdrawal age from your plan
lockedRetirementJurisdiction: Original pension jurisdiction (saved for future rules)
lockedRetirementNote: Before the age above, this balance grows but cannot fund spending. From that age, v1 treats it like an ordinary taxable registered account. The selected jurisdiction is retained, but v1 does not model LIF annual minimums/maximums, special unlocking, or the 50% unlocking option.
valLockedAccessAge: Earliest withdrawal age must be between {{min}} and {{max}}
valLockedPartnerMissing: Choose yourself as owner until partner mode is enabled
valLockedEmployeeExceedsSavings: Your DC contribution cannot exceed annual savings
nonRegBookHint: Use your verified adjusted cost base, including reinvested distributions and purchases. If you do not know it, choose Unknown; a guessed percentage cannot support precise capital-gains tax. Your cost can exceed today's value.
nonRegYieldHint: The defaults below suit most people - leave them as-is if unsure. Interest, dividends and ETF distributions in a non-registered account are taxed the year they are paid even when auto-reinvested - that is tax drag. In retirement it joins your taxable income; during working years it is taxed at the marginal rate below. Broad equity ETFs distribute ~2%; bonds/GICs more. Set 0 to disable.
mixNote: Presets set a real return and volatility from FP Canada-style assumptions.
mixWhyConservative: These aren't a pessimistic guess: they're FP Canada's Projection Assumption Guidelines, the same forward-looking standard used by professional planning software like Snap Projections. They look conservative next to history and next to well-known stock-pickers on purpose. A diversified equity index actually returned roughly 6-7% real over the last century, but forward-looking guidelines assume less because today's valuations are higher than the historical average - that's the whole point of forecasting instead of extrapolating the past. A stock-picker's track record (Warren Buffett's included) is alpha from selection and leverage, not a market return, so it isn't a fair comparison for a passive portfolio. The GIC assumption is a decades-long forward rate, not today's 1-year rate: it will look low while rates are elevated and look right again once they normalize.
feesHint: Every account's return is reduced by this rate. FP Canada assumptions are gross of fees - net returns require subtracting them: broad index ETFs run ~0.2%, bank mutual funds often 2%+, and a 2% MER can turn a 4% withdrawal rate into a 2% one.
cppStartAge: CPP/QPP start age (60–70; QPP up to 72)
fhsaToggle: Use an FHSA (First Home Savings Account)
fhsaNote: FHSA - first-home savings account: contributions are tax-deductible like an RRSP; used to buy a qualifying first home, the full amount (plus growth) comes out tax-free like a TFSA. If you don't buy within 15 years, it automatically rolls into your RRSP tax-free. Enter the combined total for both spouses here.
fhsaContributionHint: Standard limit: $8,000/year per person, with one year of carryforward (up to $16,000 in a single year); lifetime cap $40,000/person.
fhsaOpenedYearsAgoHint: Drives the 15-year maturity clock - unlike a TFSA, FHSA contribution room only starts building the year the account opens.
fhsaTerminalRrsp: Based on {{n}} year(s) since opening, matures in {{year}} (age {{age}}) and automatically rolls into your RRSP tax-free.
fhsaTerminalPurchase: Will flow tax-free toward your home's down payment when you buy at age {{age}}.
prNote: Sale is tax-free (principal residence exemption); proceeds become investable.
saleSavingsHint: Annual savings is after existing mortgage payments. If you sell before FIRE, the linked loan’s avoided scheduled payments are added to savings from the sale year until the original loan term ends. Adjust your savings if new housing costs replace them.
prCardNote: The home you live in: sale is tax-free (principal residence exemption), no rental income.
prFundingOrderHint: The down payment is funded FHSA → TFSA → non-registered → RRSP, in that fixed order (not configurable). Non-registered gains and RRSP withdrawals are taxed.
prNetHoldingCost: Net change in holding cost ($/yr, can be negative)
prNetHoldingCostHint: Your annual living-cost change from owning this home, excluding the mortgage payment (already handled below) — e.g. property tax and maintenance minus any rent you'd otherwise be paying. Negative if owning nets out cheaper.
ipCardNote: Rented out / investment use: rent is taxed as ordinary income, half the sale gain is taxed.
ipNote: On sale, half the gain above the ACB is taxed; sales happen at the start of the chosen year, including before FIRE. Net rent is taxed as ordinary income and stops the year the property sells; don’t double-count rent inside "annual savings".
success: Your plan works - money lasts to age {{age}}.
whenNever: No FIRE age through {{age}} works with the current inputs.
numberAnswer: Your FIRE number: about {{amount}} in investable assets at the moment you retire at {{age}}.
incomeChartNote: Stacked areas are gross cash sources; the dashed line is tax paid. A GIS layer (tax-free supplement) appears from 65 when taxable income is low enough; a CCB layer (tax-free, if you've entered children) can appear from FIRE age.
taxChartNote: Stacked areas split this year's tax proportionally across taxable components — each slice is that source's share of total taxable income, scaled against the year's actual tax. Not a statutory split (all income is taxed together on one bracket ladder), but the slices always sum to the tax line in the chart above. Hover a point to see total taxable income, the average rate and the marginal bracket (computed per person, since Canada taxes individuals).
strategyNote: Ranked by after-tax estate value: at death the remaining RRSP/RRIF is fully income in the final year (when no spousal rollover is left) and half of unrealized non-registered gains is taxed - strategies that park a large RRSP to the end get taxed heavily here. The RRSP→RRIF conversion itself is not a taxable event.
timingAlready: Your current start ages are already optimal for this plan.
timingNote: Deterministic scan of start ages for the primary person; longevity risk not included.
modeledSuccessUnverified: The modeled balance lasts to age {{age}}, but this path needs checks before it can be called feasible.
lockedWithdrawalUnverified: Locked DC/LIRA withdrawals are modeled by age only. LIF limits and transfer rules have not been verified for this plan.
lockedRecommendationUnranked: A modeled path funds the spending, but locked-account withdrawal limits are unverified. No strategy or start-age recommendation can be applied.
mcSuccess: Pass rate under these model assumptions
mcError: Simulation failed. You can run it again.
mcNote: How to read it: the dark line is the median of 1,000 runs; the shaded band spans the 10th–90th percentile - 8 out of 10 runs land inside, and the band's lower edge is close to the "unlucky script". The dashed red line is the actual balance path of the single run that ran out earliest - it drops to zero before the 10th-percentile band does, because at that age fewer than 10% of runs had failed yet; that line is where the "worst run" figure in the text above comes from. Your accounts hold the same market, so every account shares each year's draw (correlation) - splitting money across wrappers does not cancel volatility. Read this rate as the share of simulated paths that did not need an adjustment under these assumptions: below 100% means some scripts require spending cuts or extra income, not bankruptcy. It is also sensitive to the return assumption - half a percentage point can move it several points, so don't treat single digits as precise. These percentages are sensitivity signals under the current model, not a recommendation threshold.
mcIdle: What is Monte Carlo? The charts above assume the same return every year, but real markets have good and bad years. Monte Carlo randomizes each year's return (scaled to your asset-mix volatility) and reruns your entire plan 1,000 times, counting how often the money lasts to life expectancy - that's the success rate. It exposes the big blind spot: a bear market in the first years after FIRE (sequence-of-returns risk) hurts far more than a late one. Click the button to run.
scenarioHint: Save a snapshot, then change inputs (retire later, spend less…) to compare.
disclaimer: Educational estimate only, today's dollars, simplified tax rules - not financial advice.
simplificationsNote: This calculator makes a number of simplifying assumptions — results are an approximation, not a guarantee of reality.
targetUnset: You did not set a personal asset target in the questionnaire. Enter one here to compare; this is not the calculated FIRE amount you need.
targetLate: Short: about {{amount}} at {{fireAge}} vs target {{target}}; saving on, you reach it at age {{age}}.
targetNever: With current savings and returns, {{target}} is never reached.
targetHint: Includes proceeds from planned property sales (principal residence tax-free, investment-property gain taxed; unsold real estate doesn't count); if short, saving is assumed to continue. Assets at FIRE are measured at the start of that year; sales at that age close first. Whether the money lasts for life is what the other modes answer.
meltdownNote: After any required RRIF minimum, the model draws RRSP funds for spending up to the selected income ceiling (lowest bracket by default), then non-registered → TFSA. If those run out, it returns to RRSP; the ceiling cannot guarantee a tax bracket or avoid OAS recovery tax.
terminalTaxBreakdown: Final-year taxable addition: remaining registered {{registered}} + taxable gains {{gains}}. Added final-return tax and repayment {{tax}} (including additional OAS recovery {{oas}}); separate probate fee {{probate}}.
terminalEstimateNote: This after-tax estate value estimates a shared projected endpoint. It adds remaining registered balances and taxable unrealized gains to the final year's modeled income. It does not model which partner dies first, spousal rollovers, or beneficiary designations, so it is not a person-by-person final return or a complete death scenario.
terminalUnsupported: An after-tax estate estimate is unavailable because required income or capital-gain tax facts are not fully modeled for this plan.
dwzGoalNote: Under Die with Zero, strategies are ranked by sustainable annual spending.
strategyNoteDwz: Ranked by sustainable spending: the highest real annual spending each strategy can sustain to life expectancy, ending near zero - the less tax paid, the more you can spend.
dwzNote: In today's purchasing power - returns are inflation-adjusted, so constant real spending already covers inflation.
dwzRiskWarning: For reference only, not a recommendation to apply directly: this is a zero-margin theoretical ceiling that assumes every year hits the expected return exactly - once Monte Carlo adds real volatility back in, its success rate is often low. Run the Monte Carlo simulation below first to check the real odds before using this number.

rrsp.title: RRSP - Registered Retirement Savings Plan
rrsp.body: Contributions deduct from taxable income now; growth is tax-deferred; withdrawals are fully taxed as income. Best filled at high-income years and drained at low-income years. Must convert to a RRIF by the end of the year you turn 71. For FIRE: the low-income bridge years are the golden window to drain it cheaply (see meltdown).

rrif.title: RRIF - Registered Retirement Income Fund
rrif.body: The RRSP's exit form: the RRSP must convert to a RRIF by the end of age 71 (the conversion itself is tax-free) - but 71 is only the deadline; you can convert earlier to match your retirement timeline, or convert only part of it. From the next year, age-based minimum withdrawals are mandatory (about 5.28% the year you turn 72, rising to 20% at 95): each withdrawal is added to that year's taxable income, and the mandatory minimum is usually exempt from withholding tax - but exempt from withholding isn't the same as tax-free, so this calculator computes the actual tax owed directly regardless of what's withheld. Anything pulled beyond that year's spending is reinvested after tax in a non-registered account. Couples can elect at RRIF setup to use the younger spouse's age for the minimum calculation, deferring tax further (the election is irrevocable) - this calculator applies it automatically, always using the younger spouse's age. An oversized RRSP forces big taxable withdrawals - the core reason to meltdown early.

withholding.title: Withholding tax
withholding.body: A lump-sum RRSP withdrawal has income tax withheld at source in tiers (outside Quebec: 10% up to $5,000, 20% from $5,001-15,000, 30% above $15,000; Quebec adds its own provincial withholding on top of the federal one). This is only a prepayment, not the final bill - at tax time the withdrawal is added to that year's total income and taxed at your marginal rate, with the withheld amount credited against it. A RRIF's mandatory minimum withdrawal is usually exempt from withholding, but it's still fully taxable income. This calculator doesn't model withholding timing at all - it computes the actual tax owed for the year directly, regardless of what was withheld.

tfsa.title: TFSA - Tax-Free Savings Account
tfsa.body: Contributions are after-tax, but growth and withdrawals are completely tax-free, and withdrawn room comes back the next year. The most flexible wrapper in Canada: withdrawals never touch taxable income or trigger OAS clawback. Usually the last account to draw from. In the withdrawal order it always goes last: let the tax-free compounding run longest, keep it as your only zero-tax-consequence cash source late in life, and it passes tax-free at death.

nonreg.title: Non-registered account
nonreg.body: A plain investment account with no tax wrapper: interest is fully taxed, eligible dividends get a credit, and 50% of realized capital gains (sale price minus ACB) is taxable. Where money goes once TFSA and RRSP room is full. In the withdrawal order it is usually spent first (after the RRSP's low-bracket room) - the only wrapper that keeps leaking taxable income, so the longer it sits the more it leaks.

acb.title: ACB - Adjusted Cost Base
acb.body: What you originally paid for your non-registered assets ("book cost" at your broker). Tax applies to 50% of (sale price − ACB). Higher ACB = smaller gain = less tax. Cash and GICs have ACB equal to face value. Entering 0 makes the calculator treat the whole balance as profit and badly overstates tax.

cpp.title: CPP / QPP - Canada / Quebec Pension Plan
cpp.body: The work-based government pension (QPP in Quebec). The amount depends on your best 39 years of contributions between 18 and 65, relative to the YMPE ceiling. Standard start at 65; as early as 60 (−0.6%/month) or as late as 70 (+0.7%/month, +42%). Retiring early dilutes the average - FIRE folks rarely get the maximum.

oas.title: OAS - Old Age Security
oas.body: A residence-based pension, independent of work: 40 years in Canada after age 18 earns the full amount (~$9,024/yr in 2026, +10% automatically at 75), fewer years prorate. Starts at 65, deferrable to 70 (+0.6%/month). High income triggers the clawback.

gic.title: GIC - Guaranteed Investment Certificate
gic.body: A term deposit: locked term, guaranteed rate, no principal risk. Interest is fully taxed annually in a non-registered account, so GICs are more tax-efficient inside a TFSA or RRSP. Not to be confused with GIS (the low-income supplement).

ympe.title: YMPE - Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings
ympe.body: The earnings ceiling for CPP/QPP contributions and benefits (~$71,300 in 2025). Earning at or above the YMPE makes that a full-credit year. The CPP estimator’s "% of the cap" refers to this.

meltdown.title: RRSP Meltdown
meltdown.body: Deliberately draining the RRSP during the low-income window after FIRE, keeping each year's taxable income within the lowest bracket (whatever room CPP/OAS leaves), to avoid two future tax events: forced RRIF minimums pushing you into higher brackets, and the remaining balance being taxed at the top rate at death. Note: the RRSP→RRIF conversion itself is tax-free, so there is no need to empty it by 71 - the remainder simply dribbles out via RRIF minimums; over-withdrawing just pays extra tax. The "meltdown ceiling" offers three settings: the lowest bracket (default, most conservative), the second bracket, or the OAS clawback threshold - raising it helps large RRSPs empty faster in the early low-income years, reducing future RRIF-forced withdrawals and the fully-taxable balance at death, at the cost of somewhat more tax paid along the way.

clawback.title: OAS Clawback (recovery tax)
clawback.body: Net income above a threshold ($95,323 in 2026) claws back OAS at 15% of the excess; around $155,000 it reaches zero. Large RRIF withdrawals are a common trigger - avoiding it is one goal of withdrawal-order planning.

fire.title: FIRE - Financial Independence, Retire Early
fire.body: Accumulating enough invested assets that passive income covers living costs, allowing exit from mandatory work before traditional retirement age. The key levers: savings rate, retirement spending, and withdrawal strategy.

dwz.title: Die with Zero
dwz.body: A life choice: rather than maximizing an estate, spend the money while alive - target the highest stable spending that lasts exactly to life expectancy. Under this goal the calculator ranks strategies by sustainable annual spending; less tax paid means more to spend. Note that this "max sustainable spending" is a theoretical ceiling computed assuming every year hits the expected return exactly - it has zero safety margin by construction. Real markets have good years and bad years, and Monte Carlo's success rate for this exact number is often noticeably low - always run Monte Carlo before applying it.

montecarlo.title: Monte Carlo simulation
montecarlo.body: Instead of one fixed return, market returns are randomized each year and the plan is simulated thousands of times, yielding a success rate. It exposes sequence-of-returns risk: a bear market in the first years after FIRE hurts far more than one later.

estate.title: Estate taxation (deemed disposition)
estate.body: Canada has no formal estate tax, but at death assets are deemed sold: the remaining RRSP/RRIF is fully income in the final year (unless rolled to a surviving spouse) and 50% of unrealized non-registered gains is taxed. TFSA and the principal residence pass tax-free. Non-registered holdings and unsold real estate also owe **probate / estate administration fees** (province-dependent — roughly 1.5% in Ontario, 1.4% in BC, up to 1.7% in Nova Scotia (the highest), a few hundred dollars flat in Alberta and Quebec, nothing in Manitoba); RRSP/RRIF/TFSA with a named beneficiary bypass it entirely. That is why after-tax estate value — net of both the death-year tax and probate — is the honest comparison metric.

principalresidence.title: Principal Residence Exemption
principalresidence.body: Capital gains on your primary home are entirely tax-free - one of the largest tax breaks in Canada. In a FIRE plan, downsizing releases a large tax-free lump sum that becomes investable. Investment properties do not qualify.

withdrawalorder.title: Withdrawal order (decumulation strategy)
withdrawalorder.body: Which account you tap first in retirement can swing the after-tax outcome by hundreds of thousands. Rule of thumb, three layers: 1) RRSP first in low-income years, capped within the lowest bracket (see meltdown) - it's tax-deferred, the bill comes eventually, so pay it in your cheapest years; 2) non-registered next - the only wrapper that keeps leaking taxable income, so the longer it sits the more it leaks; 3) TFSA always last: growth is permanently tax-free (highest-quality compounding - let it run longest), withdrawals never push up your bracket or trigger the clawback (your only zero-tax-consequence source of cash late in life, after RRIF minimums fill your brackets), and it passes tax-free at death. The comparison card below quantifies each order with your own numbers.

bridge.title: Bridge period (FIRE → pensions)
bridge.body: The years between FIRE and the start of CPP/OAS: no salary, no benefits yet - the lowest-taxable-income window of your life, and the prime hunting ground for the RRSP meltdown. A longer bridge needs more self-funded cash but gives more room to drain the RRSP at low rates; the 'defer CPP/OAS' advice only works if the bridge is funded.

sequencerisk.title: Sequence-of-returns risk
sequencerisk.body: The same average return with bad years in a different order gives wildly different endings: a bear market in the first years after FIRE forces you to sell assets at the bottom to live, and the damaged principal never recovers; the same bear at 80 is nearly harmless. It is early retirement's biggest hidden risk - invisible in fixed-return charts, and the main thing the Monte Carlo success rate measures.

realdollars.title: Today's purchasing power (real vs nominal)
realdollars.body: This calculator runs entirely in real dollars: every amount is stated in today's purchasing power and returns are net of inflation. The benefit: a number in any year compares directly to your life today - "spending 100k a year" still buys today's 100k worth at 80. Switch to Nominal display to see future face values (rising each year); purchasing power is identical.

splitting.title: Income splitting (couples)
splitting.body: Canada taxes individuals, so under progressive rates the same household income split across two returns pays far less than piled on one (two personal amounts, two runs up the low brackets). Couple mode assumes an ideal 50/50 split. Reality check: before 65, RRSP withdrawals are taxed to the account owner only and cannot be split - an even split during the bridge requires both spouses to hold comparable RRSP balances, which unbalanced couples should fix in advance with spousal RRSP contributions. After 65, the real pension income splitting rule only covers RRIF-type eligible pension income and caps at 50% to a spouse - this calculator treats all taxable income (CPP, rent, non-registered gains, etc.) as ideally splittable, which is more optimistic than the real rules.

marginalrate.title: Marginal tax rate
marginalrate.body: The rate on your next dollar of income - not the average on all of it. Canada's brackets are progressive: only the slice above each threshold pays that bracket's rate. Planning is largely about controlling the marginal rate - the meltdown keeps RRSP draws in the lowest bracket, while the clawback acts as a hidden extra 15% marginal rate at higher incomes. Ontario residents also face the surtax and health premium on top (see the entry); Quebec residents face the RAMQ premium and FSS contribution (see the entry).

correlation.title: Return correlation
correlation.body: Whether two investments move together. Your TFSA, RRSP and non-registered accounts usually hold the same markets - in a bear market they fall together, so spreading money across account wrappers diversifies nothing. The Monte Carlo here applies the same yearly market draw to every account precisely so wrappers aren't mistaken for diversification (that mistake would inflate the success rate). What actually lowers volatility is the asset mix (stocks vs bonds), not the account shell.

mer.title: MER - management expense ratio
mer.body: The share of assets a fund silently deducts every year (you never see a bill, but it is real). Broad index ETFs charge ~0.05-0.25%; actively managed bank mutual funds commonly 1.5-2.5%. Over 30 years a 2% fee consumes roughly forty percent of the final portfolio. This calculator treats return assumptions as gross of fees and subtracts the rate you enter separately.

taxdrag.title: Tax drag
taxdrag.body: The non-registered account is the only wrapper that leaks tax: interest, dividends and yearly ETF distributions are taxed even if you withdraw nothing (foreign dividends also lose a 15% withholding tax), steadily eroding compound growth. TFSA/RRSP growth is untouched - which is why withdrawal-order wisdom says not to let non-registered money linger. The calculator adds your distribution yield to each year’s taxable income; reinvested distributions raise the ACB so they are not taxed again at sale.

agecredit.title: Age amount
agecredit.body: A tax credit for those 65+: the federal amount is up to $9,208 in 2026 (reduced at 15% of net income above ~$46,400, gone near $107,800), with provincial amounts on top (ON $6,342, BC $5,927, AB $6,345; Quebec folds it into a combined family-tested retirement credit). It matters for meltdown planning: keeping taxable income under the phase-out start saves each person well over a thousand dollars a year. The calculator applies it automatically from 65.

pensioncredit.title: Pension income credit
pensioncredit.body: The first $2,000 of eligible pension income each year earns a federal credit (provinces add their own amounts). Employer pension annuities qualify at any age; RRIF withdrawals only from 65 — which is why planners suggest drawing at least $2,000 a year from a RRIF after 65: that slice is nearly tax-free. RRSP withdrawals never qualify at any age. The calculator applies the credit automatically: employer pensions at any age, RRSP/RRIF draws from 65.

gis.title: GIS - Guaranteed Income Supplement
gis.body: A tax-free top-up for low-income seniors, paid only while receiving OAS and income-tested on income that excludes OAS itself. July-September 2026 publishes a different amount and cut-off for each household shape, and this calculator uses the shape that applies: up to $1,123.17/month with a $22,800 cut-off for a single pensioner; up to $676.09/month each with a $30,096 combined cut-off when both spouses receive OAS; up to $676.09/month with a $42,144 combined cut-off for a pensioner whose 60-64 spouse receives the Allowance; and up to $1,123.17/month with a $54,624 combined cut-off for a pensioner whose spouse receives neither OAS nor the Allowance - the case a single cut-off used to misprice. The first $5,000 of employment income is exempt from the test, plus half of the next $10,000. A hidden benefit for FIRE folks: TFSA withdrawals are completely invisible to it, so an early retiree living on TFSA and already-taxed capital after 65 can report near-zero income and collect the full amount; capturing it usually means an essentially empty RRSP before 65 and deferring CPP to 70. Not to be confused with a GIC. Couples with an age gap get an often-missed extra: the 60-64 spouse of a GIS recipient can claim the Allowance - also tax-free, income-tested on combined household income, up to $1,428.06/month, reducing from $8,800 of combined income and ending at $42,144. The Allowance reduces from the published $8,800 of combined income and ends at $42,144; the pensioner-side GIS on that row falls too rather than staying flat, which is what keeps the household amount continuous when the Allowance ends. The reduction between the maximum and the cut-off is a piecewise-linear fit to the published tables of monthly amounts, and the maximum, the income cut-off and the top-up income cut-off are the published figures reproduced exactly; at any published bracket boundary the modelled amount is within $1.00/month for a single pensioner, $2.00 for two pensioners, $3.00 for the Allowance row and $1.81 for the spouse with neither, so a mid-range figure can differ from the official table by up to about $3/month. The tables are pinned in the rule pack shown under "Assumptions".

surtax.title: Ontario surtax & health premium
surtax.body: Ontario's two stealth add-ons: (1) the surtax - once provincial tax itself passes ~$5,800 it is increased by 20%, and by a further 36% past ~$7,400, effectively multiplying high-income provincial marginal rates by 1.2-1.56x; (2) the Ontario Health Premium - up to $900 per person per year, tiered on taxable income. Both settle on the tax return; they are why Ontario feels more expensive than its bracket table suggests. The calculator applies both automatically for ON residents.

rent.title: Rental income (taxation)
rent.body: When an investment property is kept for its cash flow instead of sold, the net rent (rent minus property tax, insurance, maintenance, management and other operating costs) is 100% taxable as ordinary income — no 50% capital-gains discount, no dividend credit. Enter the net figure here: during accumulation it is taxed at your working marginal rate and saved into the non-registered account; in retirement it joins taxable income and counts against tax brackets, the OAS clawback and the GIS income test. The sell-vs-hold trade-off: holding keeps the appreciation but the income is heavily taxed and the accrued gain is still taxed at death; selling crystallizes the gain once (half taxable) in exchange for rebalanceable financial assets.

baristafire.title: Barista FIRE — semi-retirement
baristafire.body: FIRE without fully stopping: quit the main career and cover part of your spending with part-time work, a small business or odd projects, so the portfolio only funds the gap. The leverage is dramatic — $20k/yr less drawn from the portfolio is, by the 4% rule, roughly $500k less capital you need to save, often years of retirement gained. The income is taxed as ordinary income, but at retirement-level income the marginal rate is low; after 65 it also enjoys the GIS work exemption (the first $5,000 doesn’t count against the income test, and only half of the next $10,000 does). A sibling concept, Coast FIRE: once compounding alone will reach your number, stop saving and earn just enough to cover current expenses. This calculator models it as a fixed pre-tax annual amount over an age range starting no earlier than FIRE. In couple mode it's taxed entirely on you, not split with your spouse the way an RRSP withdrawal or rent can be — employment-type income can't legally be shared — and only your own OAS is subject to its clawback.

debt.title: Debt amortization and inflation
debt.body: Mortgage and loan payments are contractually fixed in nominal dollars: the same paper amount every year. This calculator works in today’s purchasing power throughout, so the real burden of that same payment shrinks year after year — at 2% inflation, the final payment of a 25-year mortgage weighs only ~61% of today’s. That is the honest mechanism behind "inflation pays your mortgage"; ignoring it overstates debt pressure and pushes your FIRE age out. The engine back-solves the implied interest rate from (balance, annual payment, years remaining) and amortizes year by year; expressed in real dollars, retirement-phase payments add to the spending target and the outstanding balance is subtracted from net worth. Note the semantics of "annual savings": it is what you save after debt payments, so a loan paid off before FIRE affects the balance sheet, not retirement cash flow. A mortgage can also be attached directly to a specific property instead of this general list — the sale then automatically pays it off from the proceeds first, and while held, its interest (not principal) is deductible against that property's rental income, matching how leveraged rentals actually work. Enter each mortgage in one place only, not both.

qclevies.title: RAMQ premium + FSS contribution (Quebec retirees)
qclevies.body: Two easily-missed costs for Quebec retirees, settled on the tax return: (1) the RAMQ prescription-drug-insurance premium — anyone without private drug coverage (the common case once you leave an employer, which is most FIRE'd retirees) defaults onto the public plan and pays for it based on reported income, up to about $770/person/year in 2026; (2) the FSS (Fonds des services de santé) contribution — levied on retirement, investment and capital-gains income (OAS excluded), 1% of the amount over roughly $18,500 up to a $150 cap, then another 1% past roughly $64,355 up to a $1,000 cap. Both are per person and settle in one lump sum at tax time; the calculator applies them automatically for QC residents. Assumption: no private drug plan after retirement (true for most FIRE'd retirees who lose employer benefits) — if you keep private coverage, your actual RAMQ premium is zero.

fhsa.title: FHSA - First Home Savings Account
fhsa.body: A first-home savings account that works like an RRSP going in and a TFSA coming out: contributions are tax-deductible, and growth compounds tax-free inside. Withdraw it for a qualifying first home (must move in within a year as your primary residence) and the entire amount — contributions plus growth — comes out with no tax at all; buying an investment property does not qualify and the full withdrawal becomes taxable. Contribution room is $8,000/year plus one year of carryforward (up to $16,000 in a single year), $40,000 lifetime per person, and — unlike a TFSA — room only starts building the year the account is opened. The account itself closes at the earliest of 15 years after opening, age 71, or a qualifying withdrawal; if you never buy, the full balance rolls into your RRSP automatically, tax-free, with no effect on RRSP contribution room. It can be combined with the HBP to fund the same home purchase. This calculator models it as a single combined household bucket rather than a fourth account type, since its lifecycle always ends in a lump-sum move to a home purchase or the RRSP.

hbp.title: HBP - Home Buyers' Plan
hbp.body: A separate first-home program: withdraw up to $60,000 from your RRSP tax-free toward a qualifying home, then repay it back into the RRSP over 15 years (missed repayments count as taxable income that year). It can be used alongside the FHSA for the same purchase. Not modelled here — between the FHSA already covering most of a typical down payment and the complexity of tracking a 15-year repayment schedule, it's left out as a deliberate simplification; a down payment funded some other way understates the FHSA's tax advantage.

ccb.title: CCB - Canada Child Benefit
ccb.body: A tax-free monthly benefit for each child under 18, income-tested on adjusted family net income (AFNI): up to $8,157/yr per child under 6 and $6,883/yr per child 6-17 (2026-27 benefit year), reduced once AFNI passes $38,237 and again past $82,847, at rates that climb with the number of children (7-23% in the first band, 3.2-9.5% in the second). Like the GIS clawback, this creates a real marginal cost to RRSP withdrawals during the bridge years — every extra dollar pulled from an RRSP raises AFNI and quietly shrinks the benefit, which the withdrawal-strategy comparison accounts for automatically. Several simplifications apply. Scope: only calculated from your FIRE age on (pre-FIRE CCB is assumed already folded into "annual savings", so it isn't double-counted); federal only, no provincial top-ups like Quebec's Family Allowance; no Child Disability Benefit; no shared-custody 50% split (halve the result yourself if custody is shared); and only already-born children can be entered, not planned future ones. Calculation: AFNI is approximated by this calculator's own household taxable income for that same year (it includes OAS, unlike the GIS test, and never sees TFSA withdrawals) — the real CCB is instead paid every July based on the prior year's tax return, a one-year lag this calculator ignores (same simplification as GIS); a child's age band switches on a whole year rather than the actual birthday month; the reduction is computed with a continuous formula rather than CRA's rounded flat deduction, within $1 of the official figures; the underlying dollar amounts are assumed to track inflation exactly, so they stay constant in this calculator's today's-dollar terms; and eligibility conditions (tax residency, primary caregiver status) are assumed met.

simplifications.title: What this calculator simplifies
simplifications.body: To keep the math tractable and auditable, this calculator makes a number of simplifications; the results are a directionally honest approximation, not a guarantee of your actual future tax outcome. Couple mode assumes CPP, RRSP withdrawals, rental income and investment income can all be split 50/50 — in reality, RRSP withdrawals before 65 are taxed only to the account owner (unless you've set up a spousal RRSP ahead of time), Barista FIRE side income can't legally be split with a spouse (the calculator already handles this case separately), and the estate tax bill is estimated as an even split between spouses rather than the survivor's own single-filer bracket (usually heavier). Non-registered distributions and net rent are taxed as ordinary income every year (no dividend gross-up/credit, no rental CCA depreciation modelled); GIS and the 60-64 spousal Allowance use a piecewise-linear fit to the official tables of monthly amounts, within $3/month at every published income bracket (the maximums and cut-offs are exact); TFSA/RRSP contribution room isn't checked and RRSP refunds aren't automatically reinvested; CPP enhancement (post-2019 contributions) isn't modelled, understating younger users' benefits (a conservative direction); debts and mortgages are treated as fixed nominal payments with no refinancing or variable rates; Monte Carlo draws one shared market outcome per year across all accounts (full correlation), when real-world correlation is somewhat lower (also conservative); large one-off costs like long-term care aren't modelled; and some Quebec RAMQ/FSS figures and provincial probate-fee rates are approximated from secondary sources rather than official year-by-year data, since the official sites block automated fetching. Employer pensions add their own simplifications: survivor percentages aren't modelled (both spouses are assumed to reach the shared life expectancy), Quebec's provincial rule that pension splitting requires age 65+ is ignored (splitting stays idealized at any age), a partially-indexed pension only erodes from its start age (deferral-period erosion isn't modelled), and DC/LIRA balances entered in the RRSP field ignore LIF withdrawal caps. The FHSA's contribution deduction isn't modelled as a separate refund either (same simplification as the RRSP one above); the Home Buyers' Plan (HBP) isn't modelled at all; a planned home purchase's down payment is always funded FHSA then TFSA then non-registered then RRSP, a fixed order that isn't configurable; and the net holding-cost-change field is whatever you enter (e.g. property tax and maintenance minus rent saved) — it excludes the mortgage payment, handled separately. The Canada Child Benefit (CCB) is only computed from FIRE age on, federal only (no provincial top-ups or Child Disability Benefit), doesn't split for shared custody, uses this year's household income with no one-year lag (like GIS), and its reduction formula is continuous rather than CRA's rounded figures (within $1) — see the CCB glossary entry for the complete list.

dbpension.title: Employer pension (DB/DC)
dbpension.body: Workplace registered pension plans come in two kinds. Defined benefit (DB): a formula — often 2% × years of service × best-5-year average salary — pays a lifetime annuity, sometimes indexed to CPI, sometimes with a bridge benefit to 65. Defined contribution (DC): an investment account that is often locked in on leaving employment, for example as a LIRA. Enter that balance in the separate Locked DC/LIRA account, not RRSP/RRIF. In v1 it grows but cannot fund spending before the plan's stated earliest withdrawal age; afterwards it is treated as ordinary taxable registered money. LIF annual minimums/maximums and special unlocking are not modelled.

lockedretirement.title: Locked DC pension / LIRA
lockedretirement.body: A DC pension or Locked-in Retirement Account (LIRA) is tax-deferred retirement money that generally cannot be freely spent like an RRSP. This calculator's v1 boundary model uses the earliest withdrawal age on your plan statement: before that age, the balance can grow but has zero withdrawal capacity; from that age onward it enters the ordinary taxable registered withdrawal path. The original pension jurisdiction is stored for a later LIF model, but v1 deliberately does not model jurisdictional annual minimums/maximums, hardship or small-balance unlocking, or one-time 50% unlocking.

bridgebenefit.title: Bridge benefit
bridgebenefit.body: A temporary top-up many DB pensions pay from the pension start age until 65, roughly standing in for the CPP/OAS you can't collect yet. It stops at 65 regardless of when your CPP actually starts — plan for the income step-down. Not to be confused with the bridge period (the FIRE-to-government-benefits years).

whenExplain: Method: for each age starting from today, the plan is fully simulated as if you FIREd that year - with your withdrawal strategy, property-sale plan and CPP/OAS start ages - through age {{life}}. An age counts as feasible only if the after-tax spending of {{spending}} is covered every single year without the money running out; shown is the first age that passes.
timingWhy: Why the start age matters: taking CPP early discounts it (starting at 60 pays only 64% of the age-65 amount) and deferring boosts it (142% at 70); OAS starts no earlier than 65 and grows to 136% at 70. But waiting means a longer bridge funded from your own assets. Which wins is not obvious - the tables below fully simulate each choice through age {{life}}.

displayModeNote: All amounts are today's purchasing power - the engine uses inflation-adjusted real returns, so constant real spending already keeps pace with inflation; this toggle only changes how numbers are displayed, not the calculation itself.

numberHave: With current savings and your property plan, you are projected to hold about {{amount}} at {{age}} -
numberExplain: Method: a binary search for the minimum investable assets at age {{age}} that lets the plan - with your withdrawal strategy, property-sale plan and CPP/OAS settings - spend through age {{life}} without running out. Assets are assumed split like your current TFSA/RRSP/non-registered mix (account tax treatment matters). Because government benefits and the home sale are counted, this is usually far below the crude "25× spending" rule.
yearTableNote: Where each year's money comes from, how much tax, at which bracket - audit-grade detail. Amounts are always today's purchasing power (brackets are defined in real terms); taxable income is per person after income splitting; marginal rate = federal + provincial statutory bracket (QC abatement applied). Rows marked ! have a spending shortfall. From 65 the tax math automatically includes the age amount and pension income credit (the age amount shrinks as income rises).
mcFailStats: Anatomy of the unlucky scripts: {{count}} runs failed ({{pct}}%) - the worst went broke at {{earliest}}, the typical failed run at {{median}}.
mcFailWhy: Failed runs averaged {{failed}}%/yr over the first 5 post-FIRE years, versus {{succeeded}}% for successful runs - the unlucky script is almost always the same one: a bear market right after retiring forces selling at the bottom to fund spending, and the damaged principal never recovers (sequence-of-returns risk). Late bear markets barely hurt.
mcNoFail: All {{n}} runs lasted to life expectancy - no failing scripts.
privacyNote: All financial inputs stay in your browser and are never uploaded. Anonymous usage statistics (page views, feature clicks) are collected via Google Analytics.

guidedOasAge65Detail: If you need the income or may qualify for the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS), test age 65 first.

household.title: Household and goal
household.help: Start with the timeline you want to test.
household.question: What kind of retirement are you planning?
household.why: Ages define how long you save, how long investments must fund life, and when benefits can begin. Stopping work and starting benefits are separate decisions.
household.how: Use current ages and the province where you expect to live for tax purposes.
household.example: Sam is 40, stops full-time work at 55, starts CPP at 65, and tests the plan through age 95.

income.title: Income and savings
income.help: Translate your real saving habit into one annual amount.
income.question: How much do you actually add to investments?
income.why: New deposits grow the portfolio before retirement. Salary alone does not tell us what remains after tax and daily life.
income.how: Compare account statements over the past 12 months and add deposits, excluding investment growth and transfers.
income.example: $2,000 deposited each month becomes $24,000 per year.

accounts.title: Accounts and contributions
accounts.help: Identify the tax wrappers that hold your investments.
accounts.question: Where is your retirement money today?
accounts.why: TFSA, RRSP and non-registered accounts can hold the same funds, but withdrawals and taxes behave differently.
accounts.how: Use current market balances from bank or brokerage statements. Do not enter contribution room, your home, RESP assets or future benefits here.
accounts.example: A $100,000 investment worth $80,000 when purchased has a $20,000 unrealized loss; cost is not the same as market value.

housing.title: Property and debt
housing.help: Separate a valuable home from cash available for spending.
housing.question: How will housing affect retirement cash flow?
housing.why: A home contributes to net worth, but only a sale produces spendable portfolio cash. Mortgages and rent affect annual spending.
housing.how: Choose renting, owning, or a planned purchase. Enter a mortgage with its property only once.
housing.example: An $800,000 home kept for life adds net worth but does not automatically fund groceries.

spending.title: Retirement spending
spending.help: Express the life you want in today’s purchasing power.
spending.question: What would one retirement year cost?
spending.why: This target drives withdrawals. The engine separately calculates tax and account funding needed to deliver it.
spending.how: Start from monthly essentials and add irregular annual travel, health and home costs. Exclude loans already entered elsewhere.
spending.example: $3,000 per month becomes $36,000 per year before separately modelled debt payments.

benefits.title: Benefits and assumptions
benefits.help: Connect government and employer income to the timeline.
benefits.question: What income arrives after work stops?
benefits.why: CPP/QPP and OAS can reduce portfolio withdrawals later, but the portfolio must bridge the years before they begin.
benefits.how: Use the annual age-65 estimate from My Service Canada Account or Retraite Québec. Multiply a monthly age-65 amount by 12; do not enter an already early/late-adjusted payment as the age-65 base.
benefits.example: $1,000 per month at age 65 is a $12,000 annual age-65 estimate.

review.title: Review and read results
review.help: Check the core inputs and any warnings, then read the plan conclusion before exploring detailed charts and scenarios.

questionnaire.strategyIntro: This sets the model's order for funding each year's after-tax spending. Required RRIF minimums come first. There is no best order for everyone; compare the outcomes in your results.

strategyDetails.meltdownPaced: After the RRIF minimum, draw RRSP funds toward the income ceiling (currently: {{cap}}); then use non-registered → TFSA → RRSP if needed. Aims to spread taxable withdrawals, but the ceiling is not a hard limit when other funds run out. You can change it in the results.
strategyDetails.nonRegFirst: After the RRIF minimum, use non-registered investments → RRSP → TFSA. Keeps tax-free TFSA assets for later; selling non-registered investments may realize taxable capital gains.
strategyDetails.tfsaFirst: After the RRIF minimum, use TFSA → non-registered → RRSP. TFSA withdrawals generally add no taxable income now, but use tax-free assets sooner and may shift RRSP tax to later years.
strategyDetails.rrspFirst: After the RRIF minimum, use RRSP/RRIF for spending before non-registered → TFSA. Reduces registered balances earlier, but larger taxable withdrawals may raise tax and income-tested benefit reductions.

family.essential: Start with who the plan covers and the timeline you want to examine.
family.why: Ages set saving years, retirement years and when income can begin. Province affects the tax estimate.
family.help: Use current ages and the province used for tax. The planning horizon is a range to test, not a prediction of lifespan.
family.example: Alex is 40, stops full-time work at 55 and tests the plan through age 95.

saving.essential: Count money newly added after tax, daily costs and existing loan payments.
saving.why: New deposits grow the portfolio before retirement; salary or market growth is not the same as savings.
saving.help: Review 12 months of deposits, subtract money taken back out, and exclude transfers between your own accounts.
saving.example: $2,000 a month of net new deposits equals $24,000 a year.

assets.essential: First identify the account type, then use today’s balance—not contribution room.
assets.why: TFSA, RRSP and non-registered are tax wrappers; funds and stocks are investments held inside them.
assets.help: Use a recent bank or brokerage market value. Exclude RESP, your home and future government benefits.
assets.example: A $100,000 non-registered balance with $80,000 cost has a $20,000 unrealized gain, not a $20,000 tax bill.

housing.essential: Describe where you expect to live before entering property values or loans.
housing.why: A home adds net worth but cannot pay bills unless sold. Loan payments reduce annual cash flow.
housing.help: Use the latest mortgage statement and enter each loan only once with the related property.
housing.example: A home kept for life remains net worth; its $2,000 monthly mortgage is a separate cash-flow cost.

spending.essential: Use today’s prices. Loan payments already entered elsewhere stay outside this budget.
spending.why: This is the after-tax lifestyle the portfolio must fund; the engine separately estimates withdrawals and tax.
spending.help: Start with recent spending and adjust categories that genuinely change after work ends.
spending.example: $3,000 a month is $36,000 a year before separately modelled loans.

income.essential: Identify whether income is a government benefit, lifetime employer pension, or account balance.
income.why: Income starting later reduces withdrawals later, while investments must bridge the years before it begins.
income.help: Use age-65 CPP/QPP estimates from Service Canada or Retraite Québec; do not re-enter an already adjusted claim amount as the age-65 base.
income.example: $1,000 per month at age 65 is a $12,000 annual age-65 estimate.

preferences.essential: Facts may be estimated; preferences must be chosen and confirmed by you.
preferences.why: Keeping spending fixed and exploring a maximum spending level answer different questions and carry different trade-offs.
preferences.help: Choose the comparison that reflects your intent. Unsupported legacy amounts and lifetime gifts remain disclosed wishes, not hidden engine constraints.
preferences.example: You can view a spending ceiling without applying it to your existing budget.

be12.title: RRSP contribution room
be12.explanation: Copy the lines from your CRA RRSP deduction limit statement. Leave any line blank if you cannot confirm it: a blank line stays unknown and limits precise advice, and it is never treated as zero or as unlimited room.
be12.unusedUndeducted: Contributions made but not yet deducted

be12.deductLater: Deduct this contribution in a later year

be12.retainedHelp: Room is never exceeded and the money does not disappear: the remainder stays in the non-registered account instead.
be12.savingsShare: This year's savings split also sends {{amount}} CAD to the RRSP, so that amount is already included in the planned and retained figures above.
be12.unknownRoom: Contribution room is not confirmed, so no contribution is priced. Enter the CRA statement lines to see an exact figure.

be12.overContribution: The statement's unused contributions exceed its deduction limit by {{amount}} CAD. Available room is zero; confirm the over-contribution with CRA.
be12.noOwnAccount: Assign this person their own RRSP account in the ownership section above before planning a contribution.

be12.deferred: {{amount}} CAD uses room now and is deducted in {{year}}.

be12.spousalExplanation: A premium paid to a spousal plan can be attributed back to the contributor when the plan holder is paid. Record the year each premium was actually paid, who paid it and the amount. The plan holder is the annuitant; the other person is the contributor.
be12.spousalHistory: Premium history recorded for this plan
be12.spousalDeductLater: Deduct this premium in the following year

be12.spousalWindow: A payment in {{year}} can be attributed by a premium paid in {{years}}: the payment year or either of the two preceding years.
be12.spousalBaseYearNote: Each premium is attributed at most once. A premium paid before {{baseYear}} counts as not yet attributed, because the projection starts at {{baseYear}} and no earlier payment out of the plan is recorded.
be12.spousalNoHistory: No premium history is recorded for this plan, so a payment cannot be attributed. Until you record it, the payment is not assumed to belong to the plan holder.
be12.spousalPaymentTest: Preview a payment out of this plan (CAD)
be12.spousalSplit: Attributed to {{contributor}}: {{attributed}} CAD. Taxed to {{annuitant}}: {{taxed}} CAD.
be12.spousalUnsupported: Attribution is not supported for this plan: {{reason}}

A recorded premium history marks the account as a spousal plan, so a spousal RRIF is split at the year's required minimum while a spousal LIF is refused; the couple voluntary-savings RRSP split, RRSP/RRIF age-71 conversion and multi-account destination allocation remain unsupported.
be12.spousalRrifNote: The registered type is RRIF, so the year's required minimum is taxed to the plan holder and only the excess over it can be attributed to the contributor.

be36.title: FHSA contribution room
be36.explanation: FHSA participation room belongs to the account holder, so it is recorded per person. Copy the opening year, the previous contributions and the unused room from the CRA participation-room statement or the T4FHSA slips. Leave a line blank if you cannot confirm it: a blank line stays unknown, no contribution is priced against it, and it is never treated as zero or as a full $8,000 of room.
be36.noAccount: This person has no FHSA account of their own, so there is no participation room to price. An FHSA is never shared, and a household total is not divided between two people.
be36.ambiguousAccount: This person has more than one FHSA account, so a planned contribution cannot be attributed to one of them.
be36.multipleActive: More than one FHSA is active this year. This estimate prices one active FHSA per plan, so the projection stops until only one account has a plan or a balance.
be36.openedYear: Year the first FHSA was opened
be36.priorContributions: Contributions and RRSP transfers before this plan year (CRA statement)
be36.openingRoom: Unused participation room carried into this plan year (CRA statement)
be36.openingRoomNote: Enter the room left over from earlier years, not the participation-room statement's figure for this year: that figure already includes this year's own room.
be36.scheduledRecorded: A scheduled contribution of {{amount}} CAD is recorded for this plan year, so the plan shown is the larger of that schedule and the recorded amount.
be36.ledger: Opening room {{opening}} + this year's room {{addition}} − contributions {{applied}} = closing room {{closing}} CAD
be36.lifetime: Lifetime limit {{limit}} CAD: {{used}} used, {{remaining}} remaining. Investment growth never counts against it, and a transfer is never deducted twice.
be36.retainedHelp: Participation room is never exceeded and the money does not disappear: the remainder stays in the non-registered account instead.
be36.unknownRoom: FHSA participation room is not confirmed, so no contribution is priced: {{reason}}
be36.maturity: This FHSA has reached its 15-year participation clock. The statutory rollover into an RRSP/RRIF is not implemented yet, so no contribution is priced for that year.
be36.limit: The published $8,000 annual limit, $40,000 lifetime limit and $8,000 participation-room carryforward maximum come from the CRA FHSA pages. The year's room is this year's $8,000 plus at most that carryforward maximum, and the lifetime limit bounds that whole total, so room carried in from earlier years is never spent on top of the remaining lifetime room. Not implemented yet: the 15-year / age-71 clock, rollover into an RRSP/RRIF, qualifying and non-qualifying withdrawals, home-purchase eligibility and the death event. FHSA re-participation room, designated amounts and the excess-FHSA-amount tax are out of scope too, so this ledger reports only room the published limits allow.
be36.scope: FHSA room is tracked per person and per year. Maturity, rollover, withdrawals and home-purchase eligibility remain outside this estimate.

be27.title: TFSA contribution room
be27.explanation: TFSA contribution room belongs to the person, not to an account: one CRA figure covers every TFSA you hold, so it is recorded per person and priced per person. Copy the available contribution room from your CRA account and record any TFSA withdrawal you made. Leave the room blank if you cannot confirm it: a blank line stays unknown, no new contribution is executed against it, and it is never treated as unlimited room or as zero.
be27.availableRoomNote: Enter the CRA figure for this plan year, as of January 1. That figure already contains the year's annual dollar limit and every withdrawal you made in an earlier year, so this ledger adds nothing for the year's own limit and does not restore those earlier withdrawals a second time.
be27.withdrawalsHelp: Withdrawals made since that figure restore room in the following year, never in the year of the withdrawal. A direct transfer between your own TFSAs is not a withdrawal and is not recorded here.
be27.ledger: Opening room {{opening}} + this year's addition {{addition}} + restored room {{restored}} − contributions {{applied}} = closing room {{closing}} CAD
be27.savingsShare: The plan contributes {{amount}} CAD to this person's TFSA this year, from the resolved savings split.
be27.restoredNext: Withdrawals recorded for {{year}} restore {{amount}} CAD of room in {{nextYear}}, not in {{year}}.
be27.retainedHelp: Contribution room is never exceeded and the money does not disappear: the remainder stays in the non-registered account instead.
be27.unknownRoom: TFSA contribution room is not confirmed, so no new contribution is executed and the money is retained: {{reason}}
be27.limit: The CRA states that contribution room is the annual TFSA dollar limit plus unused room from previous years plus withdrawals made in previous years (excluding direct transfers). That is the rule this ledger recomputes. The annual dollar limit itself is not encoded: it is indexed in $500 increments and no sourced limit pack is published, so a year after the statement year adds no room here and says so instead of guessing.
be27.scope: Not implemented yet (BE-27 B), so no cash is routed by them here: the retirement surplus refill and cash-flow surplus policy, the RRIF-forced-surplus reinvestment interaction, the surplus-strategy comparison, and internal compliant transfer handling.

benefitCategoryTitle: GIS and Allowance: which household row applies

coverageLimitation.capitalGainsInclusion: The 66.67% rate proposed in 2024 was cancelled and never took effect; the rate is statutory and not year-switched.
coverageLimitation.federalAgeAmount: The income test uses taxable income rather than net income, and the amount is a pinned 2026 figure.
coverageLimitation.federalBasicPersonalA: The phase-out uses taxable income, not the net income the CRA worksheet uses.
coverageLimitation.federalIncomeTaxBrack: Quebec applies its 16.5% abatement on top, which is its own row.
coverageLimitation.federalPensionIncomeA: Eligibility by income type is the caller’s job; the amount is not year-switched.
coverageLimitation.federalSpouseAmount: Applied only when a spouse net income is supplied, and it draws on the same basic personal amount as the credit above.
coverageLimitation.manitobaBpaPhaseOut: The phase-out bounds are not part of the T4032 chart and are a pinned figure.
coverageLimitation.ontarioHealthPremium: The segments are pinned 2026 figures, not year-switched.
coverageLimitation.ontarioSurtax: The two thresholds are pinned 2026 figures, not year-switched.
coverageLimitation.peProvincialIncomeTax: Resolved 2026-09-15: the CRA T4032-PE July 2026 guide governs this ladder — its fourth threshold is $142,520 (replacing January’s $142,250) and its over-$200,000 rate is 20% — and the CRA July PDF above is the document a reader can check. The Prince Edward Island government’s own page is cited as an additional source, but a real browser is sent to a Radware CAPTCHA, so this row marks it as blocked and no figure here depends on it.
coverageLimitation.probateFees: Pinned 2026 figures read from the cited TaxTips.ca table; provinces whose fee is tiered (BC, AB, PE, NL, NS, NB) are simplified to one flat amount plus rate matching the top tier.
coverageLimitation.probateFeesApproxNT: Pinned 2026 figures read from the cited TaxTips.ca table; provinces whose fee is tiered (BC, AB, PE, NL, NS, NB) are simplified to one flat amount plus rate matching the top tier. This build charges Yukon’s $140 flat filing fee rather than the territory’s own published tiers (the Northwest Territories publishes a tiered fee rising to $435), so the priced fee is an explicit approximation that is understated above the first tier.
coverageLimitation.probateFeesApproxNU: Pinned 2026 figures read from the cited TaxTips.ca table; provinces whose fee is tiered (BC, AB, PE, NL, NS, NB) are simplified to one flat amount plus rate matching the top tier. This build charges Yukon’s $140 flat filing fee rather than the territory’s own published tiers (Nunavut publishes a tiered fee rising to $425), so the priced fee is an explicit approximation that is understated above the first tier.
coverageLimitation.probateFeesMB: Pinned 2026 figures read from the cited TaxTips.ca table; provinces whose fee is tiered (BC, AB, PE, NL, NS, NB) are simplified to one flat amount plus rate matching the top tier. Manitoba abolished its probate fee on 2020-11-06, so the correct priced fee is exactly zero and the cited table documents the elimination.
coverageLimitation.provincialAgeAmount: Pinned 2026 figures, and the income test uses taxable income rather than the net income the TD1 worksheet uses.
coverageLimitation.provincialBasicPerson: An assumed future year indexes it from the pack’s own policy; the 2026 value is the published one.
coverageLimitation.provincialPensionInco: Not year-switched, and applied with no income test in this model.
coverageLimitation.provincialSpouseAmoun: The amount is `min(max, threshold − spouse net income)`, which is algebraically identical to the TD1 worksheet because every such form publishes `max + low = threshold`; the real gap is the spouse net-income base, and the maxima and thresholds are pinned 2026 figures.
coverageLimitation.quebecBasicPersonalAm: The linked Ministry of Finance parameters PDF carries the 2026 basic personal amount this build prices. The 2026 ladder whose bottom rate credits it — 14% up to 54,345 dollars, then 19%, 24% and 25.75% — is printed in the CFFP Guide des mesures fiscales, listed as an additional source. Revenu Québec’s own rates page is cited too, but it answers automated readers with HTTP 403, so the CFFP guide and this note are what let a reader check the rates.
coverageLimitation.quebecFssContribution: The legacy preview applies it to taxable income; the person-owned Quebec path uses the Schedule F base. The two caps (150 dollars and 1,000 dollars) are not printed in the linked parameters PDF.
coverageLimitation.quebecIncomeTaxBracke: The linked Ministry of Finance parameters PDF carries the 2026 thresholds this build prices. The full 2026 ladder — 14%, 19%, 24% and 25.75% above those thresholds — is printed in the CFFP Guide des mesures fiscales, listed as an additional source. Revenu Québec’s own rates page is cited too, but it answers automated readers with HTTP 403, so the CFFP guide and this note are what let a reader check the rates.
coverageLimitation.quebecProvincialAgeAm: Pinned 2026 figures; applied on taxable income per person rather than through Schedule B’s family-income test, which this build does not compute. The 18.75% reduction rate is printed in the CFFP *Guide des mesures fiscales* listed as an additional source.
coverageLimitation.quebecProvincialPensi: Pinned 2026 figures; the retirement-income amount is priced only inside the 65+ combined credit and shares the same per-person Schedule B approximation as the age amount.
coverageLimitation.quebecRamqPremium: The priced figures are a legacy preview, not a 2026 published schedule: the linked guide prints the 2025 table (5,000 band at 7.84%/11.76%, 392 base, 755 maximum, 19,890 single threshold), which this build indexes by 2% to $20,288 and $770 because Revenu Québec has not published the 2026 tax-year Schedule K. The linked document therefore does not itself print the priced figures.
coverageLimitation.yukonBpaPhaseOut: Mirrors the federal enhanced-BPA phase-down and is a pinned figure rather than a chart line.
coverageLimitation.quebecFederalAbatemen: A pinned statutory share, not selected by tax year. No 2026 CRA form is published yet, so the cited form is the most recent edition that prints the 16.5% rate; the Department of Finance report carries it for 2026.
